title: Massive French Worker Protests Flood Streets, Demand Government Change – CBS News
body:
Thousands of public‑sector employees poured onto the streets of France on Thursday, staging one of the largest coordinated walkouts in recent memory. From teachers and railway staff to municipal workers and hospital personnel, an estimated 80,000 to 100,000 people abandoned their posts to demand higher wages and relief from a cost‑of‑living squeeze that has left many French households struggling to make ends meet. The demonstrations, which stretched from Paris to regional cities such as Lyon, Marseille and Lille, featured a mix of peaceful rallies, symbolic “strike” rallies and, in some locales, sporadic clashes with police over barricades and crowd‑control measures.

The protest wave is the latest chapter in a series of nationwide actions that have been building since the spring, when France’s government unveiled a series of fiscal reforms aimed at curbing public spending and reducing the deficit. While the administration argues that the measures are necessary to preserve France’s social model, unions contend that the reforms disproportionately affect low‑ and middle‑income workers, eroding real wages at a time when inflation remains stubbornly high. According to the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE), consumer prices have risen by 5.6 % over the past year, outpacing the 2 % wage growth recorded for public‑sector employees.

Union leaders from the Confederation Générale du Travail (CGT), the French Democratic Confederation of Labour (CFDT) and the National Union of Education (SNU) coordinated the strike through a series of joint statements, emphasizing that the action is not merely about pay but also about broader socioeconomic grievances. “We are confronting a government that talks about solidarity while imposing austerity on those who keep the country running,” said CGT spokesperson Marie‑Claire Dubois during a rally outside the Ministry of Labour. “Our demands include a real increase in the minimum wage, a revaluation of public‑sector salaries, and measures to lower energy bills for families.”

The impact on daily life was immediate and palpable. In Paris, the metro system ran at reduced capacity, with many lines operating on a “strike timetable” that left commuters waiting up to an hour for a train. Major airports reported flight delays as ground‑handling staff participated in the walkout, while several schools in the capital and provincial towns remained closed, prompting parents to seek emergency childcare. Retail outlets in city centres experienced a surge in foot traffic, as protesters used the opportunity to voice their concerns directly to merchants and passers‑by.

Economists warn that the sustained pressure from public‑sector strikes could force the government to reconsider its fiscal roadmap. A recent survey by the Paris School of Economics found that 62 % of French voters support wage increases for public employees, even if it means higher taxes or a modest rise in public debt. However, policymakers remain cautious, pointing to the European Union’s fiscal rules that limit deficit spending and the need to maintain France’s credit rating. Finance Minister Bruno Le Maire reiterated the government’s stance, stating that “responsible budgeting and structural reforms are essential for long‑term stability,” while also signaling a willingness to engage in dialogue with union representatives.

As the protests enter their second week, the trajectory of the dispute will likely hinge on the government’s response and the unions’ capacity to maintain public support. If negotiations stall, further rounds of industrial action could target additional sectors such as the energy and postal services, amplifying economic disruption. Conversely, a constructive bargaining process could pave the way for a compromise that balances fiscal prudence with social equity. For now, the streets of France remain a vivid reminder that the battle over wages, living costs and the future of the welfare state is far from over.
